passage: Ayesha, you asked if I was scared. Let me, Kavitha, tell you. I was twenty-five when I married Paul. My parents said they wouldn't come, not because he was unkind, but because he wasn't from our community. Appa said it on the phone quietly, which was worse than shouting. On the morning itself I cried in the registrar's washroom in my mother's old silk saree, the one I'd taken without asking. I loved them. I also knew the life was mine to choose. Both things were true, and they pulled in opposite directions all day. Paul held my hand through the vows. Years later Amma told me she'd sat by the phone the whole afternoon, hurting too.

qa.q: What was Kavitha wearing when she cried in the registrar's washroom?
qa.a: She wore her mother's old silk saree, the one she'd taken without asking.

qa.q: What did Kavitha feel on her wedding day, and why?
qa.a: She felt torn: she loved her parents and was hurt by their absence, yet she knew the life was hers to choose.

qa.q: What could Kavitha offer Ayesha now?
qa.a: Honest company: telling her that mixed feelings are normal, that choosing her life doesn't mean she stops loving her family, and that the hurt may run both ways.

qa.q: What does Amma sitting by the phone all afternoon reveal about her side?
qa.a: It shows she was hurting too, perhaps longing to be there while feeling bound by the refusal.

grounding: An older woman recalls marrying outside her community while her parents refused to come, torn between love for them and her right to choose.

passage: Rain hammered the tin roof of the registrar's office in Madurai, and half the street outside was under water. Revathi wrung the ends of her dupatta and checked her phone again. Nothing from Appa. Her father, Shankar, had said it plainly a month ago: 'If you marry a boy from outside our community, don't expect us there.' She'd still saved two chairs near the front. Lokesh, soaked from the auto ride, sat beside her. "We can wait ten minutes," he whispered. She shook her head. "They're not coming. The rain isn't why." Her throat ached. She loved her father's stubborn, careful hands; she loved Lokesh; she was allowed to choose. When the clerk called their names, she stood, looked once more at the door, and walked forward.

qa.q: How many chairs had Revathi saved near the front?
qa.a: She had saved two chairs near the front.

qa.q: What does Revathi mean when she says, 'The rain isn't why'?
qa.a: She knows her parents' absence is a choice, not the weather, and saying it aloud shows her hurt and her acceptance at once.

qa.q: What might help Revathi carry both her love and her choice on this day?
qa.a: Letting herself grieve their absence openly with Lokesh while standing by her decision, instead of pretending she feels only one thing.

qa.q: What might Shankar be feeling at home as the wedding goes ahead?
qa.a: He may feel hurt and angry about her choice, and perhaps a quiet grief at missing his daughter's wedding, even if pride keeps him away.

grounding: On a stormy wedding day a young woman marrying outside her community faces her parents' refusal to attend, torn between love for them and her own choice.

passage:
Dear Amma and Appa,
The wedding is on the 14th, at the registry office, then lunch at Naveen's aunt's house. I am writing because you have not picked up my calls since I told you.
I know you think I've turned my back on our family and our ways. I haven't. I still light the lamp every Friday. I still make your rasam, Amma, badly.
But Naveen is a good man, and I am twenty-five, and this is my life. I can love you and still choose him. I didn't know it would feel like being cut in half.
If you cannot come, I will understand, and it will hurt. There will be two chairs empty.
Your daughter,
Usha

qa.q: Where will the wedding lunch be?
qa.a: At Naveen's aunt's house.

qa.q: What is Usha feeling when she writes about being cut in half?
qa.a: She feels torn and heartbroken, loving her parents while claiming her right to choose Naveen.

qa.q: What turning point could still exist at this stage?
qa.a: Keeping a door open, as Usha does with the empty chairs, so her parents can later choose to come closer.

qa.q: What might Usha's Amma be feeling reading this letter?
qa.a: She may feel hurt and afraid of losing her daughter's world, and also moved by the lamp and the rasam.

grounding: Shows a woman marrying outside her community, writing to parents who refuse to attend, torn between love for them and her right to choose.

passage:
You're asking how I'm doing? Honestly, I don't know. The wedding was beautiful. Manoj cried, which was sweet. His whole family came, his grandmother danced.
And from my side? My cousin, and two school friends. My parents didn't come. My mother said if I married a man from outside the community, I was choosing to be a stranger to them.
The thing is, I'm not angry all the time. Some days I understand. They grew up with rules that held everything together. I'm breaking one. It must feel to them like losing me.
But it feels to me like they chose a rule over their daughter. Both are true, I think. That's what makes it so heavy. I'm Sangeeta, by the way. Newly married and a bit broken.

qa.q: Who came to the wedding from Sangeeta's side?
qa.a: Her cousin and two school friends.

qa.q: What does Sangeeta mean when she says "Both are true"?
qa.a: She feels torn and heavy with hurt, understanding her parents' fear of losing her while feeling they chose a rule over her.

qa.q: What small step might help Sangeeta at this stage?
qa.a: Letting herself grieve without deciding the relationship is over, and keeping one gentle line of contact open, if it feels safe.

qa.q: What is it like for Manoj at a wedding with her parents missing?
qa.a: Manoj may feel joy and sadness mixed, happy to marry her yet aware of the empty places and her hurt.

grounding: Shows a woman whose parents refused to attend her wedding outside the community, feeling torn between loving them and choosing her life.

Before: Pooja told her parents on a Sunday that she and Jeevan, a Christian colleague, would marry in March. Her father left the table. Her mother said nothing at all.
During: The invitations went out in February. Pooja held her parents' card for three days before posting it. Her mother phoned once: "We will not be coming. Don't ask again." Pooja sat on the bathroom floor, holding the phone.
After: The wedding day was bright. Pooja laughed at the speeches and danced with Jeevan's sister. Late that night, alone for a minute, she took out her phone and looked at her mother's name without pressing it.

qa.q: Who did Pooja dance with at the wedding?
qa.a: Jeevan's sister.

qa.q: What does Pooja looking at her mother's name without pressing it suggest?
qa.a: She feels torn and aching, happy in her marriage but still missing her mother and hurt by the refusal.

qa.q: What could Pooja do at this stage to protect herself and the relationship?
qa.a: Let herself feel both joy and loss, and choose a calm moment later to send a short message, when she feels ready.

qa.q: How might Pooja's mother be experiencing the wedding day?
qa.a: She may be hurt and grieving too, holding to her refusal while knowing her daughter is marrying without her.

grounding: Shows a woman whose parents refuse to attend her wedding to a man from outside their community, torn between love and her right to choose.

subtype: Stage 1: Values clash after marriage or career [Actor]
passage: Karthik, you ask why there are no grandparents in your Kiran Athai's wedding photos. I'll tell you. I was twenty-four when I married Joseph, from a different community and a different faith. I told my parents months before. Appa said, "If you do this, we won't come." I thought he didn't mean it. On the wedding morning I kept looking at the gate of the hall, even while the vows were being said. They didn't come. I felt split down the middle: one half wanting to run home and beg, the other half knowing I had every right to choose my own life. Amma sent a sari through my cousin, no note. I wore it at the reception. Their hurt was deep, kanna, and so was mine. Both were real.

qa.q: What did Appa say when Kiran told him about the marriage?
qa.a: He said, "If you do this, we won't come."

qa.q: What was the young Kiran feeling as she watched the gate during the vows?
qa.a: She felt torn in two, longing for her parents to come while knowing she had every right to choose her life.

qa.q: When Amma sent the sari with no note, what choice did Kiran make, and what might it have meant?
qa.a: She wore it at the reception, perhaps keeping a thread of connection with Amma even while the hurt was fresh.

qa.q: What might Amma have been feeling when she sent the sari?
qa.a: Amma may have felt torn herself, hurt by the marriage yet unable to let her daughter's wedding pass with nothing from her.

grounding: Shows a young woman who married outside her community facing her parents' refusal to attend, torn between love for them and her right to choose.
